butt in: typical: butt in on sb/sth, stop butting in. NOT for: waiting.
He butted in on our conversation.
get involved in something that does not concern you
typical: butt in on sth. NOT for: being invited.
They don't want outsiders butting in.
Don't butt in on their private decision.
buy out: buy someone's share of a business so that you control it
typical: buy sb out, a buyout. NOT for: selling your share.
She bought out her business partner.
The company was bought out by a rival.
pay money so someone can leave an organization early (the army)
typical: buy sb out of sth. NOT for: staying.
He bought himself out of the army.
Her family bought her out of the contract.
buy up: quickly buy as much of something as you can
typical: buy up land/shares/tickets/stock. NOT for: buying one item.
Developers bought up most of the land.
Fans bought up all the tickets in an hour.
by comparison: shows how something looks when set beside the thing just mentioned
typical: neutral to formal, at the start of a sentence. NOT for: a sharp opposite (use 'by contrast').
Last year's results were weak. By comparison, this year looks good.
Prices in the city are high. By comparison, the village is cheap.
Our old car was noisy; by comparison, the new one is silent.
by contrast: introduces something very different from what you have just mentioned
typical: formal or written, at the start of a sentence. NOT for: only a small difference.
The north is rainy. By contrast, the south is dry and sunny.
Sales fell in Europe. By contrast, they rose in Asia.
My brother loves crowds; I, by contrast, prefer quiet places.
by the same token: says that the same argument also applies to something else
typical: formal, in an argument or discussion. NOT for: adding an unrelated point (use 'also').
If we praise good work, by the same token we should address poor work.
Customers expect quality; by the same token, they expect fair prices.
You can't blame him for failing, and by the same token you can't praise him for luck.
